data.chapter: Imperial China and the Wider World
data.section: Imperial Rule and the Ming Dynasty
data.sourcePassage:
Imperial China was ruled by dynasties — lines of rulers from the same family. A dynasty's right to rule was often explained through the Mandate of Heaven: a ruler who maintained order and prosperity could claim Heaven's support, while natural disasters or rebellion could be seen as signs that the mandate had been lost.

The Ming dynasty began in 1368 after overthrowing the Mongol Yuan dynasty. Ming rulers restored Chinese traditions of government and culture. Beijing became the main capital, and the Forbidden City — a vast imperial palace complex — placed the emperor at the centre of political and ceremonial life. The emperor was the highest authority, but governing an enormous empire required a large bureaucracy of officials who collected taxes, managed grain supplies, judged legal cases and kept records.

Many officials gained office through the civil service examination system. These tests focused on Confucian classics, essay writing and moral reasoning. The system created a route into government for some men outside the highest families, but it was not equal: only those whose families could afford years of study could realistically compete. Women were excluded entirely.

Zheng He, a Ming admiral, led large fleets across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433. His voyages reached Southeast Asia, South Asia, the Middle East and East Africa, demonstrating Chinese maritime power and diplomatic reach. These voyages show that China had major global connections before European empires dominated sea routes — and challenge the mistaken idea that world history was only shaped by European exploration.

questions.question: When did the Ming dynasty begin?
What was the Mandate of Heaven?
options: A law passed by the emperor ordering officials to pay taxes
The idea that a ruler had the right to govern if they maintained order and prosperity
A religious ceremony performed each year in the Forbidden City
A trade agreement between China and European powers
questions.modelAnswer: The Mandate of Heaven was the idea that a ruler had the right to govern if they maintained order and prosperity. Disasters or rebellion could suggest the mandate had been lost.

questions.question: Why was the civil service examination system not fully equal?
options: Only men from the imperial family were allowed to take the exams
Only those whose families could afford years of study could realistically compete, and women were excluded
The exams were only held in Beijing, making them inaccessible to most
Results were decided by officials rather than by examination performance
questions.modelAnswer: Only men from wealthy enough families who could afford years of study could realistically compete. Women were entirely excluded from the system.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about Zheng He's voyages and the history of global exploration?
options: Zheng He's voyages had no significant impact on world history
European exploration always came before Chinese exploration in every part of the world
China had major global maritime connections before European empires dominated sea routes
The Ming government encouraged Zheng He's voyages primarily to establish colonies
questions.modelAnswer: The passage argues that Zheng He's voyages demonstrate that China had major global connections before European empires dominated sea routes, challenging the idea that world history was only shaped by European exploration.

data.chapter: Imperial China and the Wider World
data.section: The Qing Dynasty and Global Trade
data.sourceTitle: The Qing Dynasty, Trade and Chinese Society
data.targetTitle: The Qing Dynasty, Trade and Chinese Society
data.sourcePassage:
The Qing dynasty began ruling China in 1644 after the Manchus from northeast Asia conquered the Ming. The Qing kept many Chinese governing traditions, including the bureaucracy and civil service examinations, while also preserving Manchu identity. Under emperors such as Kangxi and Qianlong, Qing China expanded and became one of the largest and wealthiest states in the world.

Chinese goods were famous across the world. Porcelain was prized for its quality. Silk was a valuable luxury fabric. Tea became increasingly popular in Britain and Europe. Trade connected China with Southeast Asia, the Indian Ocean world, the Middle East and Europe. However, European demand for Chinese goods created a problem: British consumers wanted tea, silk and porcelain, but Chinese merchants often wanted silver in payment rather than British manufactured goods.

Most people in Ming and Qing China lived in villages and worked in agriculture. Farming was the base of the economy. Cities such as Beijing, Nanjing, Suzhou and Guangzhou contained markets, workshops, temples and government offices. Family was central to Chinese society: respect for parents and ancestors was important, and households could include several generations. Women played important roles in household management, textile production and family networks, but men generally had more legal and social power.

Social hierarchy placed scholars and officials at the top, followed by farmers, artisans and merchants. In practice, some merchants became extremely wealthy despite officially lower status. Society was more complex than a simple ranking.

questions.question: What were three Chinese goods in high demand across the world?
options: Coal, iron and timber
Porcelain, silk and tea
Rice, wheat and cotton
Gunpowder, paper and compass

questions.question: What trade problem did European demand for Chinese goods create?
options: China produced too little tea to meet European demand
Chinese merchants wanted silver in payment, but European merchants wanted to pay in manufactured goods
Chinese ports refused to allow European ships to dock
European goods were considered too valuable to trade with China
questions.modelAnswer: European consumers wanted Chinese goods, but Chinese merchants often wanted silver in payment rather than European manufactured goods. This meant silver flowed into China rather than a balanced exchange.

questions.question: What does the passage say about merchants in Chinese society?
options: Merchants were the most respected group in Chinese society
All merchants were poor because trade was illegal in the Qing period
Merchants were officially ranked below farmers but some became extremely wealthy in practice
Merchants held the same status as government officials
questions.modelAnswer: Merchants were officially placed low in the social hierarchy, below farmers and artisans, because they made money from exchange rather than production. However, in practice some merchants became extremely wealthy and influential.

questions.question: The passage describes Qing society using a hierarchy of scholars, farmers, artisans and merchants, but then says 'society was more complex than a simple ranking'. What does this suggest about using such categories in history?
options: The ranking was completely accurate and reflects the reality of everyone's life
Categories and official rankings can be useful guides but may not capture how real people lived
Historians should ignore official rankings entirely
Merchants were actually the poorest group in Qing society
questions.modelAnswer: The passage suggests that official categories like social hierarchies can provide a useful framework, but real life was more complex. Some people (like wealthy merchants) had much higher actual status than their official ranking implied.

data.chapter: Imperial China and the Wider World
data.section: The Opium Wars and Unequal Treaties
data.sourceTitle: Conflict, Opium and the Weakening of Qing China
data.targetTitle: Conflict, Opium and the Weakening of Qing China
data.sourcePassage:
The Qing government controlled Western trade through the Canton system, limiting most trade to one port. British merchants found this restrictive. Unable to sell enough British goods to pay for Chinese tea and porcelain, they turned to selling opium — a powerful addictive drug grown in British-controlled India — into China through smuggling networks.

The Qing government saw opium as a serious problem because addiction harmed individuals and families, silver flowed out of China, smuggling weakened respect for Qing law and foreign merchants challenged Chinese control over trade. In 1839, the Qing official Lin Zexu confiscated and destroyed large quantities of British opium in Canton. Britain responded with military force, beginning the First Opium War.

British naval technology gave Britain a decisive advantage. The war ended with the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842. China was forced to open several ports to trade, pay compensation and cede Hong Kong to Britain. This was an unequal treaty because China did not negotiate as an equal. The Second Opium War, from 1856 to 1860, forced further concessions from Qing China. These events weakened Qing sovereignty and increased foreign influence.

The Opium Wars should not be oversimplified. They involved trade, drugs, law, empire, military power and different ideas about international relations. The Qing saw their actions as legitimate defence of sovereignty. Britain claimed it was defending free trade. These different viewpoints show why studying multiple perspectives makes historical understanding stronger.

questions.question: What did Lin Zexu do in Canton in 1839?
options: Signed the Treaty of Nanjing with British officials
Confiscated and destroyed large quantities of British opium
Opened Canton as a free trade port for all nations
Led an attack on British naval ships in the harbour
questions.modelAnswer: Lin Zexu confiscated and destroyed large quantities of British opium in Canton in 1839.

questions.question: Why did British merchants start selling opium into China?
options: Opium was a legal product approved by both the British and Qing governments
They could not sell enough British goods to pay for Chinese tea and porcelain, so turned to opium for profit
The Qing government asked Britain to supply opium for medicinal use
Opium was grown in China and British merchants simply transported it
questions.modelAnswer: British merchants could not sell enough manufactured goods to pay for the Chinese goods they wanted to buy. They turned to selling opium grown in India as a way to balance the trade and make profits.

questions.question: Why was the Treaty of Nanjing described as an 'unequal treaty'?
options: It gave equal benefits to both China and Britain
China did not negotiate as an equal but was forced to accept terms after military defeat
Both sides refused to sign it
It was agreed by all Asian countries, not just China
questions.modelAnswer: The Treaty of Nanjing was unequal because China had been defeated militarily and was forced to accept terms — opening ports, paying compensation and ceding Hong Kong — without negotiating as an equal partner.

questions.question: The passage says the Qing and Britain had different viewpoints on the Opium Wars. Why is understanding multiple perspectives important when studying these events?
options: It proves that one side was completely right and the other completely wrong
It allows historians to understand why people at the time acted as they did and creates a more complete account
It means no historical judgement can ever be made about the Opium Wars
It shows that both sides agreed on all the key issues
questions.modelAnswer: Understanding multiple perspectives allows historians to explain why different actors made the choices they did. The Qing saw themselves as defending sovereignty; Britain claimed to defend free trade. Neither perspective alone gives the full picture.
